MB1: A Fock basis enumerates the allowed many-electron occupation states of a chosen set of spin orbitals. It is the discrete Hilbert-space foundation on which operators, Hamiltonians and eigenstates are represented. In XMD Quantum the basis is bounded deliberately so dimensions and memory use are checked before enumeration.
MB2: Basis restrictions reduce the determinant space to explicitly allowed occupation sectors. They are useful for fixed particle counts and configuration windows, but a restriction is only a mathematically valid symmetry reduction when the Hamiltonian preserves that projected space.
MB3: Fermionic operators implement creation, annihilation and number operations with the signs required by anticommutation. Products retain operator ordering, so the representation can build physically meaningful many-body Hamiltonians without hiding convention changes.
MB4: Wavefunctions represent amplitudes over a many-body basis and are the objects on which observables and transitions are evaluated. The roadmap tracks a richer state representation beyond the eigenvector arrays already returned by bounded solvers.
MB5: Operator algebra connects symbolic many-body terms with their numerical action on a basis. The capability includes composing fermion terms and producing sparse matrices, while the roadmap also anticipates more general matrix-free actions for larger calculations.
MB6: Generic expectation-value semantics provide a uniform way to evaluate bra-ket expressions across supported states and operators. This avoids every higher-level feature inventing a different convention for quantities such as spin, orbital moment or arbitrary observables.
MB7: Bosonic modes extend the Hilbert space beyond fermionic occupations to excitations with unbounded occupation in principle, such as phonons or photon-like degrees of freedom. Practical calculations require explicit truncation and convergence controls.
S1: Dense diagonalization constructs the complete bounded Hamiltonian matrix and solves for all Hermitian eigenpairs. It is extremely useful as an exact reference for small models because residuals and orthogonality can be checked directly, but its memory cost grows quadratically with basis dimension.
S2: Krylov and Lanczos methods build a small subspace from repeated Hamiltonian-vector products. They make low-energy states and response calculations possible without storing or diagonalizing the complete dense Hamiltonian, which is a key scaling step toward Quanty-sized problems.
S3: Low-energy-state solvers focus numerical work on the ground state and a limited excited manifold rather than the full spectrum. That is often sufficient for thermodynamics and spectroscopy when the relevant energy window is controlled explicitly.
S4: Complete ensemble semantics define how a collection of quantum states and weights becomes a physical mixed state. This matters for finite-temperature calculations, degeneracies and any observable that must be averaged over more than one initial state.
S5: Convergence controls turn numerical settings into evidence: the calculation is repeated or refined until observables change by less than a declared criterion. The goal is to distinguish a stable physical result from one that merely completed successfully.
S6: GPU Krylov moves iterative Hamiltonian-vector operations to accelerator hardware while keeping the same scientific acceptance criteria as CPU execution. Numerical speed is useful only when residual, convergence and parity checks remain explicit.
P1: Atomic multiplet physics describes correlated open-shell states in which Coulomb interactions, spin-orbit coupling and crystal fields split otherwise degenerate configurations. It is the central local-physics model behind the bounded 2p→3d spectroscopy already available in XMD Quantum.
P2: Slater integrals parameterize angular components of electron-electron Coulomb interactions. Separate direct and exchange terms let atomic and core-excited configurations reproduce multiplet structure without reducing the interaction to a single Hubbard-like number.
P3: Spin-orbit coupling links orbital and spin angular momentum and is essential for core-level splittings and magnetic dichroism. XMD Quantum treats it as an explicit one-electron Hamiltonian term with separately supplied coupling strengths where the bounded model requires them.
P4: General crystal fields describe how the surrounding electrostatic or ligand environment breaks atomic rotational symmetry. The roadmap extends beyond the bounded cubic/axial terms toward a general tensor representation that can express lower-symmetry environments consistently.
P5: Arbitrary geometry makes beam direction, sample orientation and applied-field direction explicit inputs rather than assuming fixed laboratory axes. That is required before calculated polarization dependence can be compared safely with a real experimental setup.
P6: Polarization operators determine how linear, circular or general electromagnetic polarization couples initial and final states. The current bounded atomic model has fixed-axis channels; the roadmap generalizes this into explicit reusable transition-operator semantics.
P7: Ligand and charge-transfer models enlarge the configuration space so electrons can move between a correlated local shell and ligand-like orbitals. This is necessary when a purely ionic atomic description cannot represent covalency or satellite structure.
P8: Cluster and Anderson-style models combine an interacting local subsystem with ligand or bath degrees of freedom. They bridge atomic multiplet physics toward more material-realistic impurity and cluster descriptions while retaining controlled many-body semantics.
X1: X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) computes transition strength from occupied initial states into core-excited final states as a function of photon energy. The bounded native model produces several polarization channels and an isotropic spectrum from the same explicitly defined Hamiltonians.
X2: X-ray linear dichroism (XLD) is the difference between absorption spectra for two linear polarization directions. It is sensitive to anisotropy in orbital occupation and local symmetry, so geometry and polarization conventions must be stated explicitly.
X3: X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) compares right- and left-circularly polarized absorption. The sign depends on helicity and axis conventions, which is why XMD Quantum records explicit channel definitions rather than treating XMCD as an unlabeled subtraction.
X4: Finite-temperature spectroscopy forms a Boltzmann-weighted initial-state ensemble and evaluates transitions from every retained state. Heating can therefore introduce new transitions at different energies; it is not merely a scale factor on the zero-temperature spectrum.
X5: Broadening converts discrete transition lines into a continuous spectrum that can represent lifetime and instrumental resolution. The model must keep width conventions explicit—for example Lorentzian FWHM—so comparisons do not hide normalization or factor-of-two errors.
X6: Green's functions encode frequency-dependent propagation and response through the resolvent of the Hamiltonian. Continued fractions generated from Lanczos recursions can evaluate these responses without explicitly constructing every excited eigenstate.
X7: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is a second-order process with absorption into an intermediate core-excited state followed by radiative decay into a final state. It requires incident energy, energy loss, lifetime broadening and both incoming and outgoing polarization semantics.
X8: Photoemission and inverse photoemission probe electron-removal and electron-addition spectral weight. Unlike fixed-particle-number absorption, these channels connect different particle-number sectors and therefore exercise the rectangular operator machinery directly.
X9: X-ray emission spectroscopy and non-resonant inelastic X-ray scattering add complementary response channels beyond absorption. Their transition operators and kinematic conventions need to be explicit before they can share the generic response infrastructure safely.
X10: Fluorescence yield integrates selected radiative decay channels after excitation. A reusable implementation must define which final channels are included and how the yield relates to the underlying excitation and decay response functions.
X11: ResponseFunction is the intended reusable abstraction for frequency-dependent spectra and correlation functions. It separates the general numerical response machinery from a specific experiment such as XAS, RIXS or photoemission.
M1: The bounded cluster reference is a deliberately small, controlled cluster model used to test conventions, convergence and independent Quanty parity. It is an acceptance target rather than a claim of general material realism.
M2: A general cluster Hamiltonian removes the hard-coded limits of the reference model and supports richer local, ligand and hopping structure. Scientific correctness depends on keeping orbital ordering, occupancy sectors and interaction conventions explicit.
M3: A typed tight-binding model represents orbitals, onsite terms and hoppings as a reusable material-facing object. It provides a clean bridge from one-electron electronic-structure information into the interacting many-body layer.
M4: Periodic and open clusters define whether hopping wraps across a boundary or terminates at the finite edge. The distinction affects symmetry, momentum interpretation and finite-size convergence, so it belongs in the explicit model contract.
M5: DFT/Wannier ingestion maps external electronic-structure data into XMD Quantum model parameters. The roadmap treats this as a provenance-sensitive transformation rather than silently interpreting arbitrary external files.
M6: A hybridization function summarizes the energy-dependent coupling between an interacting subsystem and its environment. It is a natural interface for impurity-style models and for material-derived bath information.
D1: A density matrix represents pure or mixed quantum states in a form suitable for ensemble averages and open-system extensions. It provides the natural state representation when a single wavefunction is insufficient.
D2: CalculateRho constructs a density matrix from states, ensembles or solver output and makes trace-based observables available consistently. It is a prerequisite for more general finite-temperature and dynamical workflows.
D3: Mean-field operators replace selected interaction terms by effective one-particle fields determined from expectation values. Their usefulness depends on an explicit self-consistency definition and clear separation from the exact interacting Hamiltonian.
D4: A mean-field ground-state solver iterates the effective Hamiltonian and density until a self-consistent fixed point is reached. Convergence criteria and metastable solutions must be surfaced rather than hidden.
D5: Ground-state evolution follows an initially prepared state under a time-dependent Hamiltonian. It enables pump, quench and field-ramp scenarios once the solver and time-dependent operator contracts are available.
D6: General time evolution propagates wavefunctions or density matrices through time. A production implementation must define integrators, error control, observable sampling and whether evolution is unitary or includes additional dissipative terms.
R1: The Python engine is the GUI-independent scientific core. It can be installed and imported separately, allowing scripts, tests, services and desktop clients to call the same calculation functions without bringing in Qt or plotting dependencies.
R2: Versioned typed models define stable request and result objects rather than passing loosely structured dictionaries throughout the product. Schema versions make breaking changes detectable and give saved calculations a durable contract.
R3: JSON contracts serialize requests and results using data-only structures. Executable objects and unknown keys are rejected, which makes saved calculations portable across the CLI, GUI and other clients without Python pickling.
R4: Provenance and evidence record how a result was produced: model parameters, engine version, diagnostics and validation context. The public dashboard publishes only sanitized derived evidence while private raw evidence remains immutable.
R5: The native-to-Quanty adapter maps a typed XMD request into an independently executable Quanty representation. It is designed to fail closed when semantics cannot be represented safely instead of silently changing the physical model.
R6: Resource limits reject calculations before they exceed explicitly bounded basis, memory or work budgets. This keeps a scientific request reproducible and prevents a client from silently degrading the requested calculation to make it finish.
R7: Linux/HPC execution means the same scientific core can run without a desktop GUI on Linux compute environments. Deployment and scheduler integration are separate from the physics contract and should not change numerical semantics.
R8: GPU execution selects supported accelerator kernels while preserving the same returned NumPy-facing result contracts and diagnostics. Explicit GPU requests fail visibly if the required backend is unavailable.
R9: Experimental Conditions is the canonical simulation context for temperature, pressure, magnetic field, polarization, geometry, sample orientation and resolution. Human-friendly presets resolve to concrete values so labels such as 'room temperature' never become ambiguous physics inputs.
V1: Independent Quanty execution runs the reference implementation separately from the native engine so agreement is meaningful evidence rather than two code paths sharing the same numerical implementation.
V2: Atomic parity tests compare native and Quanty energies, transition strengths and spectra under explicit tolerances. The evidence is bounded to the supplied synthetic acceptance models and is not a claim of validation against every real material.
V3: Finite-temperature parity extends the comparison to Boltzmann populations and thermally weighted spectra. It checks both statistical-mechanics semantics and spectral consequences of excited initial states.
V4: Geometry parity checks that beam, sample and polarization transformations have the same physical meaning across native and reference execution. This becomes important as fixed-axis assumptions are removed.
V5: Cluster parity compares controlled cluster outputs with independent Quanty execution. It validates conventions and bounded reference behavior before the cluster model is generalized further.
V6: The capability inventory audits Quanty documentation and maps discovered functionality onto implementation and roadmap entries. It prevents the parity roadmap from being limited to whichever features happen to be remembered manually.
V7: Automatic cross-validation turns independent scientific comparison into a repeatable pipeline step. New evidence can be discovered and checked continuously while unknown evidence families remain semantically neutral until reviewed.
V8: Full semantic parity is the long-term condition in which supported Quanty concepts have equivalent meaning, conventions and acceptance evidence in XMD Quantum—not merely similarly named functions.
V9: NAS evidence statistics and family discovery verify immutable evidence inventories, classify known artifact families and generate derived dashboards. Newly discovered families are surfaced automatically but are not assigned scientific meaning until a reviewed parser exists.
U1: The Python API exposes the scientific engine directly to notebooks, scripts and downstream applications. It is the clearest programmatic surface for reproducible calculations and also serves as the foundation beneath higher-level clients.
U2: The command-line interface exposes the same calculation contracts for shell and batch workflows. It is intentionally a thin client over the Python engine rather than a separate implementation of the physics.
U3: The standalone Qt GUI provides an interactive desktop client for XMD Quantum while keeping the scientific engine in a separate package. GUI fields, examples and saved requests are translated into the same typed calculation contracts used by Python and CLI clients.
U4: Workbench integration reconnects the standalone XMD Quantum product to the broader XMDWorkbench application once the scientific and product boundaries are stable enough to integrate safely.
U5: HPC and service workflows package the headless engine for remote, scheduled or service-style execution. They must preserve request, result and provenance contracts across the transport layer.
